content: The mean pain score in the intervention group (PCA tramadol) was lower compared to the mean pain score in the comparison group (PCA fentanyl). The certainty of this evidence is moderate. Fewer women in the intervention group (PCA tramadol) experienced overall side effects compared to women in the comparison group (PCA fentanyl). The certainty of this evidence is moderate. The mean expulsion time was shorter in the intervention group (PCA tramadol) compared to the comparison group (PCA fentanyl). However, the certainty of this evidence is low. Satisfaction ratings were similar between the intervention group (PCA tramadol) and the comparison group (PCA fentanyl). The certainty of this evidence is high. More women in the intervention group (PCA tramadol) required additional analgesic medication compared to the comparison group (PCA fentanyl). The certainty of this evidence is low. Draft judgment: Neither the intervention nor the comparison is clearly favored. Regarding values, there is possibly important uncertainty or variability in how much people value the main outcomes. The resource requirements (costs) are judged to be negligible or result in savings. The cost-effectiveness of the intervention does not favor either the intervention or the comparison. The impact on health equity is judged to probably have no impact. The intervention is considered acceptable to key stakeholders. The intervention is judged to be feasible to implement. For cervical priming prior to surgical abortion at less than 12 weeks, the use of mifepristone (200 mg orally 24–48 hours prior) or misoprostol (400 μg sublingually 1–2 hours prior, or vaginally/buccally 2–3 hours prior) is suggested. The use of osmotic dilators for cervical priming is not recommended. In studies comparing misoprostol to placebo, pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater in the misoprostol group. Fewer women in the misoprostol group required further dilation, and the time to complete the procedure was shorter. Fewer complications, such as cervical injury and incomplete abortion requiring re-aspiration, were observed in the misoprostol group. However, more women in the misoprostol group experienced side effects such as vomiting, diarrhea, and cramping. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes ranged from low to high. When comparing vaginal misoprostol to oral misoprostol, pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater, and fewer women required further dilation in the vaginal misoprostol group. The time to complete the procedure was shorter, and fewer women experienced nausea. However, more women in the vaginal misoprostol group experienced abdominal pain or cramping. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes ranged from very low to moderate. When comparing vaginal misoprostol to sublingual misoprostol, fewer women in the vaginal misoprostol group experienced nausea or abdominal pain/cramping. The certainty of evidence for these outcomes is low.
